content.text: Students build from Lesson 24 topic selection, Lesson 25 inquiry questions, and Lesson 26 credibility evaluation to decide which sources are most useful for uncovering a hidden innovator’s story.
Research makes hidden stories visible when students choose evidence that is accurate, relevant, accessible, and strong enough to explain contribution and impact.
Students will paraphrase from their most useful sources, organize notes by category, and begin drafting sections of their informational research writing.
Today’s work helps students narrow their research set so they can explain one innovator’s contribution, support claims with evidence, and prepare visuals for presentation.
Source List from Lesson 26
Unit 3 Lesson 27 Student Edition
Evaluate sources for usefulness in relation to a focused research topic. Compare multiple sources and select the most accessible and relevant sources for future note-taking.
Use comparative language, subordinating conjunctions, and nominalized academic vocabulary to justify why one source is more useful than another.

Students will evaluate sources for usefulness in relation to a focused research topic. Students will compare multiple sources and select the most accessible and relevant sources for future note-taking.
Students will use comparative language, subordinating conjunctions, and nominalized academic vocabulary to justify why one source is more useful than another.
Turn and Talk
Think-Pair-Share
Quick Write
Turn and Talk
Directions:
Turn and talk to discuss the answer to the question.
What might be the difference between a source that is interesting and a source that is useful?
Language Lab
Directions:

Open your source list from the previous lesson and put your finger on one source you think might help answer your inquiry question. Today, we are going to practice a sentence pattern that helps researchers explain exactly why a source is useful instead of only saying it is good or helpful.
What makes a source explanation stronger: saying “This source is useful” or naming the exact part of the source that helps answer your question? Why?
Using Relative Clauses to Explain Source Usefulness
Writers use a relative clause to show exactly what in a source makes it useful. A relative clause starts with words like
which
or
that
and adds details about the source.
Model Sentence

This museum article, which includes dated photographs, a timeline of the inventor’s experiments, and information from the museum’s archives, is a useful source for my inquiry question about the innovator’s impact because it provides accurate evidence I can verify.
What source is being evaluated in this sentence?
What part of the sentence gives more information about the source?
What do these details show about the source?
How does that help the writer judge the source?
How does the sentence connect the source back to the inquiry question?
To explain why a source is useful, we:
name the source
add a relative clause with
which
or
that
to show what it includes
explain how that evidence helps answer the inquiry question
This helps us show how the source’s evidence supports our thinking.
Now try the same structure with one source on your organizer. Start with the source name, add a relative clause, and explain how it helps answer your inquiry question.
This source, which/that ____________________, is useful for my inquiry question about ____________________ because ____________________.
Which source will you describe, and what relative clause can you add to show why it is useful?
Part A: Compare Multiple Sources
Good researchers compare sources side by side. They ask:
Which source answers my research question most directly?
Which source is easier to understand without losing important detail?
Which source includes helpful headings, captions, diagrams, or charts?
Which source adds new information instead of repeating what I already know?
Think-Pair-Share
Directions:

Choose two sources from your current list and access them. For each source, record what it helps you learn, which text features or visuals support understanding, and how well it matches one inquiry question. Don’t forget you must reference at least one piece of evidence (detail, heading, chart, or explanation from the source). Then, compare the two sources and decide which one is more useful for your research purpose right now. Finally, discuss your response to the question with a partner.
Discussion protocol:
Partner A states which source is more useful and WHY
Partner B must respond using one of the following:
“I agree because ___”
“I disagree because ___”
“I would improve your idea by ___”
Then, switch roles.
Which source seems more useful for your research question, and what makes it more useful?
Part B: Choose Useful Sources
Quick Write
Directions:

Refine your source list by marking the sources you will keep for your project. A star next to the source means to keep it. A question mark next to the source means it’s useful but missing something. An X means remove it because it’s not helpful in answering your inquiry question. Then, write one to two sentences answering the question below.
Which source are you choosing to keep, and why is it more useful than another source on your list?
Reflection (W.6.8)
Reflect on your ability to choose sources using the Reflection routine.
How confident are you in deciding which sources are most useful for your research topic?
Quick Write
Directions:
Write two to three sentences to answer the question below.
Why is it important to compare sources when conducting research?

This section shifts from identifying credible sources to evaluating how effectively those sources support a specific research purpose. Students learn that usefulness is determined not only by whether a source is accurate, but also by how clearly it answers the inquiry question, how accessible the information is for note-taking, and how well its features support understanding of key ideas such as contribution, impact, and recognition. Emphasize that researchers must make intentional decisions about which sources will best support their writing and that not all credible sources are equally useful for every stage of research. Students begin refining their source sets by prioritizing clarity, relevance, and informational value. Students also continue applying the popular media analysis work from earlier lessons by noticing whether headings, captions, diagrams, timelines, or sidebars make a source more useful for understanding the innovator’s contribution or impact.
Have students take out their source list from the previous lesson.
Turn and Talk
Say these Directions:
Turn and talk to discuss the answer to the question.
Ask:
What might be the difference between a source that is interesting and a source that is useful?

A source can be interesting because it has cool facts or images, but a useful source directly helps answer my inquiry question. A useful source gives details I can use in my notes and writing, not just information that catches my attention.
Say:
Interesting sources may include surprising facts, images, or stories. Useful sources must help students:
answer inquiry questions
collect evidence for writing
explain contribution or impact clearly
Not all interesting sources should be kept.
A source can be credible but not useful if it does not provide enough detail or does not directly help explain the innovator’s contribution or impact.
Credibility means: Can I trust it?
Usefulness means: Can I use it to answer my inquiry question?
Connection to Today's Learning
Say:
Now that you can name the difference between interesting and useful, you are ready to compare sources more carefully and decide which ones deserve a place in your research set.
Connect yesterday’s source credibility work to today’s deeper task of deciding which sources are actually useful for answering inquiry questions.

This mini-lesson strengthens students’ research explanations by teaching a sentence structure they can use immediately in source evaluation. Students learn that a relative clause begins with which or that and adds the exact source evidence that shows why a source is useful for an inquiry question.
When explaining usefulness, students should focus less on “trust” language and more on:
detail
clarity
relevance
ability to answer the question
Use credibility language only when explaining why the source is reliable, not when explaining usefulness.
Language Lab
Say these Directions:

Open your source list from the previous lesson and put your finger on one source you think might help answer your inquiry question. Today, we are going to practice a sentence pattern that helps researchers explain exactly why a source is useful instead of only saying it is good or helpful.
Ask:
What makes a source explanation stronger: saying “This source is useful” or naming the exact part of the source that helps answer your question? Why?

Naming the specific part of the source strengthens the explanation because it shows how the source helps. If I say which section, chart, quote, or detail answers my question, my explanation is clearer and more convincing.
Teach: Using Relative Clauses to Explain Source Usefulness
Writers use a relative clause to show exactly what in a source makes it useful. A relative clause starts with words like which or that and adds details about the source.
Model Sentence

This museum article, which includes dated photographs, a timeline of the inventor’s experiments, and information from the museum’s archives, is a useful source for my inquiry question about the innovator’s impact because it provides accurate evidence I can verify.
Ask:
What source is being evaluated in this sentence?
(the museum article)
Ask:
What part of the sentence gives more information about the source?
(which includes dated photographs, a timeline of the inventor’s experiments, and information from the museum’s archives)
Ask:
What do these details show about the source?
(They show that the source has specific evidence that can be checked.)
Ask:
How does that help the writer judge the source?
(It shows the source is credible and accurate because the information can be verified.)
Ask:
How does the sentence connect the source back to the inquiry question?
(It explains that the source is useful for the inquiry question about the innovator’s impact and why.)
To explain why a source is useful, we:
name the source
add a relative clause with
which
or
that
to show what it includes
explain how that evidence helps answer the inquiry question
This helps us show how the source’s evidence supports our thinking.
Say these Directions:
Now, try the same structure with one source on your organizer. Start with the source name, add a relative clause, and explain how it helps answer your inquiry question.
Display frame:
This source, which/that ____________________, is useful for my inquiry question about ____________________ because ____________________.
Ask:
Which source will you describe, and what relative clause can you add to show why it is useful?

The science museum website, which includes a labeled diagram and a short explanation of how the device worked, is useful for my inquiry question about the inventor’s contribution because it gives specific evidence I can use in my notes.
Connection to Today's Learning
Say:

Now, we have a stronger sentence structure for clearly explaining source usefulness. Next, we will compare real sources and use this same kind of thinking to decide which ones deserve a place in their research set.
Students strengthen research language by using relative clauses to connect a source’s evidence, credibility, and accuracy directly to an inquiry question.
Language Focus:
Relative clauses beginning with which and that
Source-evaluation language including useful, credible, accurate, specific, verified
Inquiry language including inquiry question, evidence, contribution, impact
Cause-and-effect reasoning with because
Before Language Lab (Preparation Step—Optional)
Students orally finish the stem “This source is useful for my inquiry question because it includes _____.
Prompt students to add information after which or that that names a real feature, detail, or evidence from the source.
If students only name a source type, press them to explain how the source’s evidence and credibility help answer the inquiry question.
You said "This site has a lot of facts"—we can say: "This site, which includes dates and verified examples, is useful because it gives specific evidence for my inquiry question."
You said "I trust this one more"—we can say: "This article, which lists the museum archive and publication information, seems more credible and accurate for my research."
This source, which includes _____, is useful for my inquiry question because _____.
I trust this source more because it includes _____, which helps me verify _____.
This source is a useful fit for my research because it helps me uncover _____ about the innovator’s contribution.
Invite students to rehearse the sentence first in their own words or in a shared home language and then recast it into the academic frame with which or that.
Validate student-generated phrases about trust and usefulness, then help students expand them into fuller academic sentences.
If students place which or that without adding source-specific information → Prompt: "What exact feature, quote, chart, or detail comes after which or that? Add the evidence right there."

If students explain usefulness with personal preference instead of inquiry relevance → Prompt: "Show how the source helps answer your question. What does it teach you about the innovator’s contribution, impact, or recognition?"

If students confuse credibility with usefulness → Prompt: "Use the relative clause to name the evidence in the source first, and then finish the sentence by explaining why that evidence is accurate or trustworthy."
Student uses which or that to add a source-specific detail after naming the source.
Student explains how the detail named in the relative clause makes the source useful, credible, or accurate for the inquiry question.
Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Relative Clauses

Model one sentence aloud and have students underline the part before the comma and circle the part that begins with which or that. Linking Evidence to the Inquiry Question: Prompt students to finish the sentence frame “This source, which includes _____, helps answer my question about _____ because _____.” Credibility and Accuracy: Remind students to look for the author, organization, date, archive, or publication information and include one of those details in the relative clause or the reason. Written Expression: Allow students to say the full sentence aloud to a partner, provide an oral recording of their explanation, or use speech-to-text tools before writing the final sentence.
Ready for extension

Invite students to write a second sentence explaining how a different useful source adds another piece of the hidden story that the first source does not show. Ask students to revise one vague explanation from earlier in the unit into a stronger explanation that uses a relative clause and more precise source-evaluation language.
Use a Language Lab routine to teach students how relative clauses beginning with
which
or
that
help them explain why a source is a useful fit for their inquiry question by linking source evidence, credibility, and accuracy in one clear sentence.
Part A: Compare Multiple Sources (W.6.8) (15 minutes)
This guided comparison helps students evaluate the usefulness of sources before deciding which to keep. Remind students that when comparing sources, focus on only three things:
Does it directly answer my inquiry question?
Does it give enough detail for my notes?
Is it easy to understand and use?
Ignore other factors for now unless they clearly help you decide.
Say these Directions:
Good researchers compare sources side by side. They ask:
Which source answers my research question most directly?
Which source is easier to understand without losing important details?
Which source includes helpful headings, captions, diagrams, or charts?
Which source adds new information instead of repeating what I already know?
Teach: Model Comparing Sources
Say:

I am comparing two sources about the same innovator. Source A gives a clear background and has short paragraphs, so it is accessible. Source B is harder to read, but in the section explaining the person’s contribution, it provides more detail and a chart showing results. While Source A helps me understand who the innovator was, Source B is more useful for explaining what the innovator did and why it mattered. That means I may keep both, but I will use them for different purposes in my research.
Think-Pair-Share
Say these Directions:

Choose two sources from your current list and access them. For each source, record what it helps you learn, which text features or visuals support understanding, and how well it matches one inquiry question. Don’t forget you must reference at least one piece of evidence (detail, heading, chart, or explanation from the source). Then, compare the two sources and decide which one is more useful for your research purpose right now. Finally, discuss your response to the question with a partner.
Discussion protocol:
Partner A states which source is more useful and WHY
Partner B must respond using one of the following:
“I agree because ___”
“I disagree because ___”
“I would improve your idea by ___”
Then, switch roles.
Ask:
Which source seems more useful for your research question, and what makes it more useful?

The museum article is more useful for my question about the innovator’s contribution because, in the section describing the invention, it explains the process step by step. The diagram and caption also make the information easier to understand than the general biography page.
Students compare sources using evidence-based criteria and explain how text features and visuals affect usefulness.
Language Focus:
Comparative language including more useful, less detailed, more accessible
Contrast connectors including while, however, compared to
Evidence-linked reasoning with because, therefore, as a result
Before Think-Pair-Share (preparation step—optional)
Students point to one heading, caption, chart, or diagram and name what information it adds.
Push students to connect a source’s usefulness to a specific inquiry question.
Encourage students to explain how a feature helps understanding, not just name the feature.
This source is more helpful because ___.
While Source A explains ___, Source B provides ___.
Compared to the other source, this one is more accessible because ___.
If students confuse accessible with easy in a vague way → Prompt: “Explain what makes it easier to use, such as clearer headings, shorter paragraphs, or labeled visuals.”
If students name a feature without explaining it → Prompt: “Tell what the chart, caption, or diagram helps you understand.”
If students compare without using criteria → Prompt: “Add one reason tied to detail, accessibility, or match to the inquiry question.”
Student compares two sources using a clear usefulness criterion.
Student explains how a text feature or visual supports understanding.
Situation
Try this
Struggling with

Interesting vs. Useful: Prompt students with “Does this source help you answer the question, or does it only make you curious?” Text-Feature Interpretation: Ask “What does this diagram show faster or more clearly than the paragraph?” Comparison Structure: Provide the frame: While Source A ___, Source B ___. Alternative Expression: Allow students to explain one comparison orally before recording it on the organizer.
Ready for extension
Ask students to identify one source they will keep for background and one for explaining their contribution, and then explain why each has a different use.
Part B: Choose Useful Sources (W.6.7) (15 minutes)
Students have now compared sources side by side. Next, they will refine their source lists and choose which sources they will keep for note-taking and writing.

Explain that refining a source list is a strong research move. Researchers do not keep every source. They keep the sources that are most useful, most accessible, and most aligned with the project's purpose. Remind students that a smaller, stronger source set will help them paraphrase, organize notes, and avoid getting overwhelmed.
Quick Write
Say these Directions:

Refine your source list by marking the sources you will keep for your project. A star next to the source means to keep it. A question mark next to the source means it’s useful but missing something. An X means remove it because it’s not helpful in answering your inquiry question. Then, write one to two sentences answering the question below.
Ask:
Which source are you choosing to keep, and why is it more useful than another source on your list?

I am keeping the encyclopedia article because it is more accessible and more detailed than the short profile I found. Although the short profile is interesting, the encyclopedia article gives a clearer explanation of the innovator’s contribution and includes headings that help me find information quickly.
Allow students to conduct further research if they find that none of their sources are useful. Students should have at least three useful resources to gather information from.
Students write concise, evidence-based judgments about source usefulness and refine their research set for future note-taking.
Language Focus:
Justification stems including “This source is useful because”
Comparative structures including more helpful, less detailed, more accessible
Subordinating structures including although, because, while
Nominalized academic vocabulary including contribution, recognition, discovery, advancement
Students orally rehearse one sentence beginning “This source is more useful because ___.”
Prompt students to justify usefulness with evidence from the source, not personal preference alone.
Encourage students to use a nominalized noun to explain what the source helps reveal about the innovator.
This source is more useful because ___.
Although this source includes ___, it is less helpful for my research because ___.
This source supports my understanding of the innovator’s contribution or recognition because ___.
If students overuse better → Prompt: “Replace better with more useful, more accessible, or more detailed.”
If students write a weak reason like “I like it more” → Prompt: “Add evidence from the source, such as a heading, detail, explanation, or visual feature.”
If students produce a fragment after because or although → Prompt: “Read it aloud and finish the idea so it becomes a complete sentence.”
Student selects a source using stated criteria.
Student writes one or two complete sentences with comparative language and evidence-based justification.
Checklist
Provide students with a confidence continuum (i.e., 1–5). As needed, model how to demonstrate a level of confidence using the continuum.
Reflection (W.6.8)
Reflect on your ability to choose sources using the
Reflection
routine.
How confident are you in deciding which sources are most useful for your research topic?
Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Criteria for Usefulness

Offer a checklist: answers my question, understandable, detailed, feature-rich, not repetitive. Comparative Reasoning: Prompt students to use the frame: This source is more useful than ___ because ___. Academic Vocabulary Precision: Invite students to replace “helped” with “explained the contribution” or “supported understanding of the discovery.” Alternative Expression: Allow students to record their one-to-two-sentence explanation orally before writing it in final form.
Ready for extension
Invite students to write an additional sentence explaining how two useful sources work together to build a more complete record of the innovator’s story.
Part A: Compare Multiple Sources (W.6.8)
Students will use the Comparing Multiple Sources organizer to evaluate how well selected sources answer inquiry questions and how text features or visuals contribute to usefulness.
Part B: Choose Useful Sources (W.6.7)
Students will refine their source list, keep the most useful sources, and write a short justification explaining why one source is more helpful than another.

This section consolidates students’ ability to justify source selection using comparative and evidence-based reasoning aligned to W.6.7 and W.6.8. Students should demonstrate that they can explain why one source is more useful than another by referencing specific criteria such as accessibility, depth of explanation, and alignment to inquiry questions. By the end of this lesson, students should be able to clearly articulate why comparing sources improves the quality of their final research product and supports stronger explanatory writing. They should also have a good idea as to how their final set of sources will help them build a complete explanation of the innovator’s story.
Quick Write
Say these Directions:
Write two to three sentences to answer the question below.
Ask:
Why is it important to compare sources when conducting research?

It is important to compare sources because some sources give more detailed or accurate information than others. For example, one website explains the innovator’s contribution in depth, while another only gives a short biography. Comparing them helps me choose the source that gives the best evidence for my notes.
Optional Sentence Starter:
Comparing sources is important because ___. While one source ___, another source ___.
Formatively assess students’ ability to explain why one source is the most useful for their research topic.
Instruct students to review the sources they decided to keep today and take notes in their
Journal
on the following prompt:
Write the title of each source and one sentence explaining what category of information it may help you with next, such as background, contribution, obstacles, recognition, or impact.

standards.description: Explain how well writers and speakers use specific language resources to present ideas or support arguments and provide detailed evidence (e.g., identifying the specific language used to present ideas and claims that are well supported and distinguishing them from those that are not), with light support.

Explain how well writers and speakers use language to support ideas and arguments with detailed evidence (e.g., identifying the precise vocabulary used to present evidence, or the phrasing used to signal a shift in meaning), with substantial support.

Explain how well writers and speakers use specific language to present ideas or support arguments and provide detailed evidence (e.g., showing the clarity of the phrasing used to present an argument), with moderate support.
Plan and deliver longer oral presentations on a variety of topics and content areas, using reasoning and evidence to support ideas, as well as growing understanding of register.
Plan and deliver brief oral presentations on a variety of topics and content areas.
Plan and deliver longer oral presentations on a variety of topics and content areas, using details and evidence to support ideas.

Expand noun phrases in an increasing variety of ways (e.g., adding comparative/superlative and general academic adjectives to noun phrases or more complex clause embedding) in order to enrich the meaning of sentences and add details about ideas, people, things, and the like.
Expand noun phrases in simple ways (e.g., adding a sensory adjective to a noun) in order to enrich the meaning of sentences and add details about ideas, people, things, and the like.

Expand noun phrases in a variety of ways (e.g., adding comparative/superlative adjectives to noun phrases or simple clause embedding) in order to enrich the meaning of sentences and add details about ideas, people, things, and the like.

content.text: Why were some contributions overlooked in historical accounts, and how can research help us build a fuller record?
